lessons.title: Critical Sections, Peterson’s Solution, and Reordering

learningObjectives.text: Explain races, critical sections, and the three critical-section requirements.
Trace Peterson’s two-process protocol and justify its mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting properties.
Analyze why instruction reordering can invalidate a software synchronization protocol on modern architectures.

materialSections.title: Cooperating processes and race conditions
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: Concurrent access can make a shared result depend on instruction interleaving.
explanation: Cooperating processes can share an address space or exchange data through shared memory or message passing. Concurrent execution can interrupt a process while it is partly complete, so shared data needs orderly access.
The producer and consumer update a shared counter. With counter initially five, interleaving increment and decrement can leave four, five, or six, even though separate execution should leave five.

materialSections.title: Critical sections and solution requirements
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: A protocol separates entry, critical, exit, and remainder work while protecting shared data.
explanation: A critical section accesses or updates shared data, such as common variables, tables, or files. While one process is in its critical section, no other process may execute its own critical section.

A correct protocol provides mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting. Disabling interrupts can prevent preemption on one core, but long critical sections, starvation, and multiple CPUs make that approach unsuitable generally.

materialSections.title: Peterson’s two-process software protocol
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: Peterson’s solution uses flags and turn to meet the three stated requirements for two processes under its assumptions.
explanation: Peterson’s solution is restricted to P0 and P1 and assumes atomic load and store instructions. The shared flag array records readiness, while turn identifies which process may enter when both want the critical section.

Each process sets its flag, gives turn to the other process, and busy waits while the other flag is true and turn favors the other process. The lecture proves mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting, with at most one entry by the other process after a request.

materialSections.title: Modern architecture and instruction reordering
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: Independent reads and writes can be reordered, producing unexpected shared-data observations.
explanation: Processors or compilers may reorder independent operations for performance. A single-threaded program can retain its expected final values, but a multithreaded shared-data program can observe an inconsistent result.

In the flag and x example, Thread 1 expects to print one hundred after Thread 2 assigns x and sets the flag. Reordering can instead expose zero, and reordering Peterson’s flag and turn assignments can allow both processes into their critical sections.

materialSections.title: Memory barriers and atomic hardware instructions
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: Hardware primitives address reordering and provide atomic state changes for synchronization.
explanation: A memory barrier makes earlier loads and stores complete and visible before later operations. In the flag and x example, barriers preserve the intended observation of one hundred by ordering the relevant reads and writes.

test_and_set returns the old Boolean value while setting the target true atomically. compare_and_swap returns the old value and changes it only when it equals the expected value; atomic variables use such primitives for uninterruptible basic updates.

materialSections.title: Mutex locks and busy waiting
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: A mutex protects a critical section by an atomic acquire followed by release.
explanation: A mutex lock represents availability with a Boolean variable. A process acquires it before entering the critical section and releases it when leaving; acquire and release must be atomic.
The simple mutex implementation uses busy waiting, so it is a spinlock. Continual looping wastes CPU cycles, especially when one core is shared by many processes.

materialSections.title: Semaphore operations and usage
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: Semaphores use atomic wait and signal operations for resource counts, mutual exclusion, and ordering.
explanation: A semaphore is an integer accessed only by indivisible wait and signal operations. Counting semaphores range over an unrestricted domain, while a binary semaphore ranges from zero to one and can serve as a mutex.

A semaphore initialized to zero can enforce S1 before S2: P1 performs S1 then signal, and P2 waits before S2. Incorrect operation ordering can permit simultaneous critical-section access or indefinite blocking; deadlock, starvation, and priority inversion are distinct concerns.

No graph cycle means no deadlock. A cycle proves deadlock when every involved resource type has one instance, but with several instances it is necessary rather than sufficient because a release can break the cycle.

materialSections.title: Prevention by invalidating conditions
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: Prevention removes one necessary deadlock condition where practical, but each protocol has trade-offs.
explanation: Mutual exclusion cannot be denied for nonsharable devices such as printers and tape drives, although sharable read-only files do not need exclusive access. Hold and wait can be broken by requesting all resources before execution or requesting only when none are held.

No preemption can be broken by releasing currently held resources if a newly requested one is unavailable. This is practical for easily saved state such as registers and memory, but not generally for printers and tape drives.

materialSections.title: Circular-wait prevention through ordering

materialSections.title: Avoidance information and safe states
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: Avoidance uses maximum claims and safe sequences to prevent entry into unsafe states.
explanation: Deadlock avoidance requires a priori information about maximum demands. A safe state has an order in which every process can obtain its remaining needs, finish, return resources, and permit the next process to finish.
A safe state is not deadlocked; every deadlocked state is unsafe, but an unsafe state is not necessarily deadlocked. Avoidance keeps the system from entering unsafe states.

materialSections.title: Banker’s data structures and algorithms
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: Banker’s algorithm uses declared maxima and a safety check before committing a request.
explanation: For multiple resource instances, each process declares its maximum use. Available records free instances, Max records maximum claims, Allocation records current grants, and Need equals Max minus Allocation.

The safety algorithm starts Work at Available and chooses an unfinished process whose Need is no greater than Work, then adds its allocation. A request first must be no greater than Need and Available; the system tentatively updates state and restores it if unsafe.

materialSections.title: Detection with a wait-for graph
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: When prevention and avoidance are absent, detection and recovery can respond after deadlock occurs.
explanation: For a single instance of each resource type, a wait-for graph has processes as nodes and an edge Pi to Pj when Pi waits for Pj. A cycle exists if and only if the system is deadlocked in this single-instance setting.
The wait-for graph is obtained by removing resource nodes and collapsing corresponding request and assignment edges. Detecting a cycle takes O(n squared) operations for n vertices.

materialSections.title: Detection with several resource instances
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: Multiple-instance detection uses Available, Allocation, Request, Work, and Finish rather than a wait-for graph.

materialSections.title: Detection example and invocation trade-off
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: The example changes from a nondeadlocked sequence to a deadlock involving four processes after P2 requests C.
explanation: With the original request matrix, P0, P2, P3, P4, P1 can all reach Finish true, so the system is not deadlocked. Adding P2’s request for one C leaves P1, P2, P3, and P4 deadlocked after P0’s resources are reclaimed.

Frequent detection responds sooner to likely deadlocks but costs computation time, especially if invoked for every immediately ungrantable request. Defined intervals are a cheaper alternative and rollback returns a preempted process to a safe state.

materialSections.title: Termination and resource-preemption recovery
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: Recovery can terminate processes or successively preempt resources, with cost, rollback, and starvation trade-offs.
explanation: Termination can abort all deadlocked processes or abort one at a time until the cycle disappears. The all-at-once method clearly breaks the cycle but may discard long computations; one-at-a-time selection considers priority, work, resources, and interactive status to minimize cost.

Resource preemption selects a victim, rolls the victim back, and avoids starving a process repeatedly chosen as victim. A total rollback aborts and restarts the process when determining a safe state is difficult.

materialSections.title: Protection, binding, and address spaces
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: Base-limit protection and staged binding separate program addresses from their eventual memory placement.
explanation: Only registers and main memory are directly accessible general-purpose storage for the CPU. Base and limit registers restrict a user process to its legal address range; for base 300040 and limit 120900, the inclusive legal range ends at 420939.

Source addresses are symbolic, compilers make relocatable addresses, and linkers or loaders bind them to absolute addresses. Binding can occur at compile time, load time, or execution time; execution-time binding needs hardware address maps.

materialSections.title: Logical addresses, physical addresses, and relocation
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: The MMU dynamically maps the user’s logical view into physical memory when execution-time binding is used.

materialSections.title: Contiguous allocation and variable partitions
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: Contiguous allocation places each process in one continuous section and manages changing holes.
explanation: Contiguous allocation typically keeps the resident operating system in low memory and user processes in high memory. Each user process occupies one contiguous memory section.

Variable partitions create holes of various sizes as processes arrive and leave. Adjacent free partitions are merged, and first fit chooses the first adequate hole, best fit the smallest adequate hole, and worst fit the largest.

materialSections.title: Paging arithmetic and address translation
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: Paging maps same-sized logical pages to physical frames and uses page number plus offset for translation.
explanation: Paging divides physical memory into fixed-size frames and logical memory into same-size pages. It avoids external fragmentation but retains internal fragmentation, and each process needs a page table after enough free frames are found.

A logical address has page number p and offset d. For 64 pages of 1024 words mapped to 32 frames, logical addresses need sixteen bits and physical addresses need fifteen bits; a 32-bit logical space with 4 KB pages has two to the twentieth page-table entries.

materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: PTBR, PTLR, TLBs, protection bits, and shared pages support practical paging.

materialSections.title: Swapping and page movement
materialSections.label: Source material
materialSections.summary: Swapping moves memory images or pages between memory and backing store under memory pressure.
explanation: Standard swapping temporarily moves a process to backing store and later brings it back, allowing physical memory to be oversubscribed. Transfer time is proportional to the amount of memory swapped.

Modern systems generally avoid whole-process swapping because it is too slow, but modified page-level swapping is common. A page out moves a page to backing store and a page in performs the reverse operation.

questions.prompt: Which relationship is explicitly listed as a way cooperating processes may share data?
questions.rationale: The lecture names both shared memory and message passing as the two ways cooperating processes share data.

duplicateComparison.normalizedPrompt: which relationship is explicitly listed as a way cooperating processes may share data

options: Both shared memory and message passing
Shared memory alone
Message passing alone
Neither shared memory nor message passing
distractorRationales: Both shared memory and message passing — This is complete: it preserves both data-sharing mechanisms named for cooperating processes.
Shared memory alone — Shared memory is one listed mechanism, but the option omits the separately listed message-passing mechanism.
Message passing alone — Message passing is one listed mechanism, but the option omits the separately listed shared-memory mechanism.
Neither shared memory nor message passing — The lecture explicitly presents both mechanisms, so denying both contradicts the stated relationship.

questions.prompt: What initial value does the full-buffer counter have in the alternative producer-consumer solution?
questions.rationale: In the alternative producer-consumer solution, the full-buffer counter begins at zero because no produced item is initially present.

duplicateComparison.normalizedPrompt: what initial value does the full buffer counter have in the alternative producer consumer solution

options: One, because a producer is about to run
Zero, because no buffer item is initially full
The buffer capacity, because it counts empty slots
Negative one, to reserve the first buffer position
distractorRationales: One, because a producer is about to run — A future producer action does not make a buffer item full before that action occurs.
Zero, because no buffer item is initially full — This is correct: the counter counts full items, and the initial buffer contains none.
The buffer capacity, because it counts empty slots — Capacity describes the buffer size or empty capacity, not the initial count of full items.
Negative one, to reserve the first buffer position — The source initializes the full-item count at zero; it does not use a negative sentinel.

questions.prompt: When one process is executing its critical section, what must be true of other processes’ critical sections?
questions.rationale: Mutual exclusion requires that no other process execute its critical section while one process is already inside.

duplicateComparison.normalizedPrompt: when one process is executing its critical section what must be true of other processes critical sections

options: They may enter when they access different variables
They may enter after updating the turn variable
None of them may execute a critical section
They must first execute their remainder sections
distractorRationales: They may enter when they access different variables — Mutual exclusion is defined by the critical-section state, not by whether the variables appear different.
They may enter after updating the turn variable — Updating turn is part of one algorithm, but it does not permit another critical section during an occupied one.
None of them may execute a critical section — This is correct: the mutual-exclusion requirement excludes all other critical-section execution.
They must first execute their remainder sections — Remainder-section execution is outside the critical section and is not the rule that enforces exclusion.

questions.prompt: Which requirement prevents choosing the next waiting process from being postponed indefinitely when no process is in its critical section?
questions.rationale: Progress prevents the decision about the next entrant from being postponed indefinitely when the critical section is empty.

duplicateComparison.normalizedPrompt: which requirement prevents choosing the next waiting process from being postponed indefinitely when no process is in its critical section

options: Mutual exclusion
Progress
Bounded waiting
The remainder section
distractorRationales: Mutual exclusion — Mutual exclusion prevents simultaneous entry; it does not address indefinite postponement of the selection decision.
Progress — This is correct: progress requires the eligible processes to determine the choice without indefinite delay.
Bounded waiting — Bounded waiting limits how long a requester waits after requesting entry, which is a different critical-section requirement.
The remainder section — The remainder section is program work outside the entry protocol, not a scheduling requirement.

Pi is ready to enter its critical section

explanations.translation: إلى ماذا يشير page-table base register PTBR؟

explanations.translation: في مثال 64 pages وكل صفحة 1024 words، كم bit يحتاج logical address؟

explanation: تعين page tables للعمليات الثلاث نفس النسخة physical من كود libc القابل للمشاركة. تعين جداول صفحات العمليات الثلاث رمز libc المقروء نفسه إلى نسخة فيزيائية واحدة قابلة لإعادة الدخول.
